en.title: The Book of De · Chapter Forty-four · The Right Half of the Tally
en.原文:
和大怨 必有餘怨 焉可以為善 

是以聖人執右介 而不以責於人 

故有德司介 无德司徹

夫天道无親 恆與善人
en.字龕:
### 介 *jiè* ／ 契 *qì* — the tally （校勘龕 · collation niche）

**字 Graph** ｜ 篆 ![介之篆](/book-assets/hosuke-laozi-en/zhuan/%E4%BB%8B.svg) ![契之篆](/book-assets/hosuke-laozi-en/zhuan/%E5%A5%91.svg)

The silk text followed here writes 執右**介** where the Wang Bi recension writes 執左**契**. The *Shuowen*: 「介，畫也。從八從人。人各有介。」 — "A boundary-line: from 八, dividing, and 人, the person — each person has his own line." And 契: 「大約也。」 — "the great covenant," a notched tally split in two, each party keeping one half as proof. Yaomiao takes the boundary as an image of restraint within oneself: keep faith, give freely, and do not turn a gift into a debt. This is the commentator's image; the graph alone does not tell us which party held which half of a tally.
en.對校:
和大怨，必有餘怨，
:
安可以為善？是以聖人執左契，
:
而不責於人。有德司契，
:
無德司徹。
:
天道無親，常與善人。
en.疏:
杳眇曰：怨者，人倫之大患者也。大怨既成，和解之餘，猶有餘恨存焉。是故聖人貴未怨而不貴既怨，貴無爭而不貴有爭。解之者以為善，不知善在未怨之先，非在已怨之後。老子言之至矣：防患於未形，不使怨成，勝於化已成之怨。此治道之上策也。

今校帛書與王弼本，其文有異，義乃益明。帛書云「焉可以為善」，王本作「安可以為善」，辭異而義同，皆言大怨既結，難以為善也。

左右之辨、介契之分，皆當審之。今所據帛書作「聖人執右介」，王本作「聖人執左契」。吳澄釋左契，以為財物之主持券，待人來合而予之；左右之制，諸家所說未一，不宜但憑左右二字遽判施受。吾讀此章，重在守信而不責報，不以所施為索取之端。水之善，利萬物而不爭；聖人主施而不責，吾以為可與水德相發明。契以存義，徹以立威。有德司介，以信聯人；無德司徹，以力取人。施予而不求其報，是謂上德；峻法以督之，是謂下德。一念之差，治亂分焉。

天道无親，恆與善人。此至公之應也，非天道之偏愛，乃善人之行自然合天之道，故天道恆在善人之側。聖人法天，守柔曰強，為而不爭，无為而治，則長生久視，天下樂推而不厭。德經四十四章至此終，自人倫德用之可行，入形上道體之玄遠，老子之書由實入虛，其序秩然。
en.疏英:
Yaomiao says: grievance is the great blight of human relations. Once a great grievance has formed, however you patch the peace, a remnant of bitterness stays behind. So the sage prizes the not-yet-grievance over the settled one, prizes no-contention over contention managed. To call the patching "good" is to miss where goodness lives: before the grievance forms, not after. Laozi has said it to the utmost — to forestall what has not yet taken shape, to never let the grievance form, is better than dissolving one already formed: the highest policy of governance.

Collating the texts: the silk text has 焉可以為善, Wang Bi 安可以為善 — different graphs, one sense: once a great grievance has formed, it is hard to call its settlement good.

The difference between left and right, and between 介 and 契, calls for care. The silk text followed here has 聖人執右介; the Wang Bi recension has 聖人執左契. Wu Cheng explains the left tally as held by the owner of the goods, who waits for another to present the matching half and then gives what is due. Accounts of the two halves differ; left and right alone do not settle who gives and who receives. I read the chapter as a call to keep faith without demanding a return, never making what one gives a means of exacting payment. Water benefits the ten thousand things without contending; the sage gives without demanding recompense. To me, the two illuminate each other. The tally keeps faith; the exacting builds awe. He who has De minds the tally, binding men by trust; he who lacks De minds the exacting, taking from men by force. To give without asking return — the highest De; to press with steep law — the lowest De. One thought apart, order and ruin divide.

The Way of Heaven has no favorites: it sides, constantly, with the good. This is the answer of utmost impartiality — not that Heaven plays favorites: the good man's conduct of itself accords with Heaven's way, and so the Way of Heaven stands constantly at his side. The sage patterns on Heaven: keeping to the soft is called strength; doing without contending; governing by non-doing — long life and lasting sight, all-under-heaven gladly pushing him forward, never tiring.

Here the Book of De ends, forty-four chapters: from the practicable De of human relations it enters the dark distance of the Dao's own body — Laozi's book goes from the solid into the empty, in due order.
en.英譯:
Patch up a great grievance, and some grievance always remains — how can that count as good?

Hence the sage holds the right half of the tally (執右介) — and does not dun anyone for it.

So: he who has De minds the tally (司介); he who lacks De minds the exacting (司徹).

The Way of Heaven has no favorites: it sides, constantly, with the good.
